item.title: The Code Breaker
item.description:
Gene Editing Ethical Considerations

  • What happens to our societal structure when endowments that came via random lottery are no longer random? What will happen to our feelings of empathy and acceptance?

Jennifer Doudna

  • Family Diary of struggles
  • Study in 2019 of more than six million articles with women as the principal author showed that they are less likely to use self-promotional terms, such as “novel” and “unique” and “unprecedented,” to describe their findings.

CRISPR

  • The one Doudna and others developed in 2012 was based on a virus fighting trick used by bacteria, which have been battling viruses for more than a billion years. In their DNA, bacteria develop clustered repeated sequences known as CRISPRs.
  • DNA as repository of genetic information was made in 1944 by Oswald Avery and colleagues at Rockefeller University in New York. By extracting DNA from a strain of bacteria, mixing it with other, they showed that DNA transmitted inheritable transformations.
  • Innovation using cross-study has been very integral in Biology.
  • Bacterias in soil are able to communicate and join when they are starved for nutrients.
  • RNA was just seen as messenger molecule that carries instructiions from DNA that is nestled in the nucleus of cells. So, small segment of DNA that encodes a gene is transcribed into snippet of RNA, which then travels to manufacturing region of the cell. Then it facilitates the assembly of proper sequence of amino acids to make a specified protien.
  • Cech and Altman discovered that there were certain RNA introns that were self-splicing.
  • Doudna used many tactics to create an RNA enzyme, or ribozyme, that could stitch together little RNA pieces. She and Szostak engineered a ribozyme that could splice together a copy a itself.
  • Transposons or jumping genes which can change their position in a genome.
  • RNA is made up of very few chemicals, so it accomplishes complex tasks based on the different ways it is folded. One of the challenges with RNA is that it’s a molecule made of only four chemical building blocks, unlike proteins, which have twenty.
  • RNA interference: Normally the genes encoded by DNA in cells dispatch messenger RNAs to direct the building of a protein. RNA interference is when small molecules find a way to mess with these messenger RNAs. It operates by deploying an enzyme called “Dicer”. Dicer sinps a long piece of RNA into short fragments. Then these fragments do a search and destroy mission: seek out a messenger molecule that has matching letters, then they use a scissors-like enzyme to chop it up. Then that genetic information carried by that messenger RNA is silenced.
  • Later spanish scientist also discribed a different virus fighting mechanism that didn’t work with RNA interference, but much more interesting.
  • Ishino found that there were five identical segments of DNA in bacterias which usually have very less amount of DNA material to begin with. So, this had to be something important. These were “spacers”.
  • Mojica named it “Clustered regularly interspaced short pallindromic repeats”
  • When he searched for spacers in previous databases, he found that those segments matched sequences that were in viruses that attacked E. Coli. Other bacterias had this crispr sequence as well.
  • Bacterias were taking the virus’s DNA and acquired immunity to that new virus.
  • DNAs and protiens alike cannot be defined just by their sequence: you need to know how its folded in terms of its structure.
  • Enzymes are protiens that spark chemical reactions in the cells of living beings. There are 5000+ biochemical reactions catalyzed by enzymes. e.g. Breaking down starches and protiens, causing muscle contractions, regulating metabolism, and in this case: cutting and splicing DNA and RNA.
  • These CRISPR associated enzymes also known as Cas. enzymes enable the system to cut and paste new memories of viruses that attack that bacteria. They create short segments of RNA called CRISPR RNA (crRNA) that can guide a scissors-like enzyme to dangerous virus and cut up its genetic material.
  • By the time Gentech was hiring Doudna, the company already was worth 100 billion.
  • RNA hairpin where Cas6 could interact with just the right sequence.
  • Charpentier, on the other hand, was more nomadic. Since she felt more like foreigner, she found more delight in her work than anything else.
  • A gene known as P53 encodes for a protein that suppresses the growth of cancerous tumors. It helps the body respond to damaged DNA and prevents cancerous cells from dividing. Cancers proliferates if something goes wrong with this gene.
  • Elephants have 20 copies of this gene and rarely get cancer.
  • Zayner, biotechnology at home.
  • Then they found anti CRISPR cas9s that would inhibit or stop the editing. That made sure that process could be much more.
  • And with gene therapy there were incidents where people died due to immune response which made it more challenging to work with and continue progress.

Highlights

One of the leaders she tapped was a postdoc named Jennifer Hamilton who, a few months earlier, had spent a day teaching me to use CRISPR to edit human genes. I was pleased, but also a bit unnerved, to see how easy it was. Even I could do it!

item.title: Steve Jobs
item.description:
Author: Walter Isaacson

Quotes from koreader

The people who are crazy enoughto think they can changethe world are the ones who do. —Apple’s “Think Different” commercial, 1997

“So does that mean your real parents didn’t want you?” the girl asked. “Lightning bolts went off in my head,” according to Jobs. “I remember running into the house, crying. And my parents said, ‘No, you have to understand.’ They were very serious and looked me straight in the eye. They said, ‘We specifically picked you out.’ Both of my parents said that and repeated it slowly for me. And they put an emphasis on every word in that sentence.” Abandoned. Chosen. Special. Those concepts became part of who Jobs was and how he regarded himself.

item.title: At the Eleventh Hour: The Biography of Swami Rama
item.description:
Author: Pandit Rajmani Tigunait

Introduction

Swamiji deserted the academic world to wander aimlessly. He mastered hatha yoga and cultivated psychic powers at the cost (in Dr. Lakhera’s view) of stunting his intellectual growth. But Dr. Lakhera did admit that Swamiji was a remarkable hatha yogi.

In 1983 he asked me to translate his book Living with the Himalayan Masters into Hindi.

You are in the body, yet you are beyond the body. Birth and death are like two commas in the poem of life. For a yogi there is nothing like death. Just as an ordinary person takes off an old tattered garmentand puts on a new one, so does a yogi cast off his worn-outbody and assume a new one.” That is how he himself left his body.

item.title: The Elon Musk Blog Series: Wait But Why
item.description:
Author: Tim Urban

I already wanted to write about these topics, for the same reason I wrote about Artificial Intelligence—I knew they would be hugely important in the future but that I also didn’t understand them well enough. And Musk is leading a revolution in both of these worlds.

He decided to go with sustainable energy. After finishing college, he enrolled in a Stanford PhD program to study high energy density capacitors, a technology aimed at coming up with a more efficient way than traditional batteries to store energy—which he knew could be key to a sustainable energy future and help accelerate the advent of an electric car industry

item.title: Old Path White Clouds
item.description:
Author: Thich Nhat Hanh

Illuminating the rivers of his body, feelings, perceptions, mental formations, and consciousness, Siddhartha now understood that impermanence and emptiness of self are the very conditions necessary for life. Without impermanence and emptiness of self, nothing could grow or develop. If a grain of rice did not have the nature of impermanence and emptiness of self, it could not grow into a rice plant.

Understanding gives rise to compassion and love, which in turn give rise to correct action. In order to love, it is first necessary to understand, so understanding is the key to liberation.

A year later, after hitting some product or usage milestones, you raise $1 million on a $10 million valuation (your typical postseed funding round, referred to as a “series A”). That debt—the original $100,000—converts into equity in the company. Given that the valuation is $10 million, and the investor put in $100,000, he now owns 1 percent of the company. From the point of the view of the investor, this is actually problematic. Say you’re the hot startup of the moment in the midst of a bubble, and you raise on some crazy valuation, such as $100 million. Well, pity our poor angel investor; he gets only 0.1 percent of the company. In essence, the better the company does, the less of it he gets. While he’s guaranteed (in theory) to get a price per share equal to follow-on investors, that’s actually a gross mispricing of his risk, as he put his money in far earlier, when the company was far riskier. Enter the investor’s great friend: the cap. The cap dictates the maximum number at which the company will be valued, for the purposes of calculating the investor’s stake when the company takes more investment capital. In our previous example, say the initial $100,000 investment had been done at a cap of $3 million. Then, despite the company’s raising later at a valuation of $10 million, the angel’s stake amounts to $100,000 ÷ $3 million = 3.3%, a much bigger slice.
